#Text=women walk ahead and their female servants and slaves follow them;
#Text=behind these walk their husbands, fathers, or brothers, with their
#Text=man-servants and slaves. [60]
#Text=
#Text= Their ordinary food is rice pounded in wooden mortars, and cooked--this
#Text= is called _morisqueta_, [61] and is the ordinary bread of the whole
#Text= country--boiled fish (which is very abundant), the flesh of swine,
#Text= deer, and wild buffaloes (which they call _carabaos_).
#Text=Meat and fish
#Text= they relish better when it has begun to spoil and when it stinks. [62]
#Text= They also eat boiled camotes (which are sweet potatoes), beans,
#Text= _quilites_ [63] and other vegetables; all kinds of bananas, guavas,
#Text= pineapples, custard apples, many varieties of oranges, and other
#Text= varieties of fruits and herbs, with which the country teems.
#Text=Their
#Text= drink is a wine made from the tops of cocoa and nipa palm, of which
#Text= there is a great abundance.
#Text=They are grown and tended like vineyards,
#Text= although without so much toil and labor.
#Text=Drawing off the tuba, [64]
#Text= they distil it, using for alembics their own little furnaces and
#Text= utensils, to a greater or less strength, and it becomes brandy.
#Text=This is
#Text= drunk throughout the islands.
#Text=It is a wine of the clarity of water,
#Text= but strong and dry.
#Text=If it be used with moderation, it acts as a
#Text=medicine for the stomach, and is a protection against humors and all
#Text= sorts of rheums.
#Text=Mixed with Spanish wine, it makes a mild liquor,
#Text= and one very palatable and healthful.
#Text=In the assemblies, marriages, and feasts of the natives of these
#Text= islands, the chief thing consists in drinking this wine, day and night,
#Text= without ceasing, when the turn of each comes, some singing and others
#Text= drinking.
#Text=As a consequence, they generally become intoxicated without
#Text= this vice being regarded as a dishonor or disgrace. [65]
#Text=
#Text= The weapons of this people are, in some provinces, bow and arrows.
#Text=But
#Text= those generally used throughout the islands are moderate-sized spears
#Text= with well-made points; and certain shields of light wood, with their
#Text= armholes fastened on the inside.
#Text=These cover them from top to toe,
#Text= and are called _carasas_ [_kalasag_].
#Text=At the waist they carry a
#Text= dagger four fingers in breadth, the blade pointed, and a third of
#Text= a vara in length; the hilt is of gold or ivory.
#Text=The pommel is open
#Text= and has two cross bars or projections, without any other guard.
#Text=They
#Text= are called _bararaos_.
#Text=They have two cutting edges, and are kept in
#Text= wooden scabbards, or those of buffalo-horn, admirably wrought. [66]
#Text=There are many native fruit-trees, such as the _sanctors_, _mabolos_,
#Text= tamarinds, _nancas_, custard-apples, papaws, guavas, and everywhere
#Text= many oranges, of all kinds--large and small, sweet and sour;
#Text= citrons, lemons, and ten or twelve varieties of very healthful and
#Text= palatable bananas. [73] There are many cocoa-palms bearing fruit
#Text= of pleasant taste--from which is made wine and common oil, which
#Text= is a very healing remedy for wounds; and other wild palms of the
#Text= forests--that do not yield cocoa-nuts, but serve as wood, and from
#Text= whose bark is made bonote, a tow for rigging and cables, and also for
#Text= calking ships.
#Text=Efforts have been made to plant olives and quinces,
#Text= and other fruit-trees of España, but as yet they have had no success,
#Text= except with pomegranates and grapevines, which bear fruit the second
#Text= year.
#Text=These bear abundance of exceedingly good grapes three times a
#Text= year; and some fig-trees have succeeded.
#Text=Vegetables of every kind
#Text= grow well and very abundantly, but do not seed, and it is always
#Text= necessary to bring the seeds from Castilla, China, or Japon.
#Text=In the Cagayan provinces are found chestnut-trees, which produce
#Text= fruit.
#Text=In other districts are found pines and other trees which yield
#Text= certain very large pine-nuts, with a hard shell and a pleasant taste,
#Text=which are called piles. [74] There is abundance of cedar which is
#Text= called _calanta_, a beautiful red wood called _asana_, [75] ebony of
#Text= various qualities, and many other precious woods for all uses.
#Text=The meat
#Text= generally eaten is that of swine, of which there is a great abundance,
#Text= and it is very palatable and wholesome.
#Text=Beef is eaten, cattle being raised abundantly in stock-farms in
#Text= many different parts of the islands.
#Text=The cattle are bred from those
#Text= of China and Nueva España. [76] The Chinese cattle are small, and
#Text= excellent breeders.
#Text=Their horns are very small and twisted, and some
#Text= cattle can move them.
#Text=They have a large hump upon the shoulders, and
#Text= are very manageable beasts.
#Text=There are plenty of fowls like those of
#Text= Castilla, and others very large, which are bred from fowls brought
#Text= from China.
#Text=They are very palatable, and make fine capons.
#Text=Some of
#Text= these fowls are black in feather, skin, flesh, and bones, and are
#Text= pleasant to the taste. [77] Many geese are raised, as well as swans,
#Text= ducks, and tame pigeons brought from China.
#Text=There is abundance of
#Text= flesh of wild game, such as venison, and wild boars, and in some parts
#Text= porcupines.
#Text=There are many buffaloes, which are called carabaos, which
#Text= are raised in the fields and are very spirited; others are brought
#Text=tame from China; these are very numerous, and very handsome.
#Text=These
#Text= last are used only for milking, and their milk is thicker and more
#Text= palatable than that of cows.
#Text=Goats and kids are raised, although their flesh is not savory, because
#Text= of the humidity of the country.
#Text=These animals sicken and die for that
#Text= reason, and because they eat certain poisonous herbs.
#Text=Ewes and rams,
#Text= although often brought from Nueva España, never multiply.
#Text=Consequently
#Text= there are none of these animals, for the climate and pasturage has not
#Text= as yet seemed suitable for them. [78] There were no horses, mares, or
#Text= asses in the islands, until the Spaniards had them brought from China
#Text= and brought them from Nueva España.
#Text=Asses and mules are very rare,
#Text= but there are many horses and mares.
#Text=Some farms are being stocked with
#Text= them, and those born there (mixed breeds for the most part) turn out
#Text= well, and have good colors, are good tempered and willing to work, and
#Text= are of medium size.
#Text=Those brought from China are small, very strong,
#Text= good goers, treacherous, quarrelsome, and bad-tempered.
#Text=Some horses
#Text= of good colors are brought from Japon.
#Text=They have well-shaped bodies,
#Text= thick hair, large fetlocks, large legs and front hoofs, which makes
#Text= them look like draft-horses.
#Text=Their heads are rather large, and their
#Text=mouths hard.
#Text=They run but slowly, but walk well, and are spirited,
#Text= and of much mettle.
#Text=The daily feed of the horses consists throughout
#Text= the year of green provender, [79] besides rice in the husk, which
#Text= keeps them very fat. [80]
#Text=
#Text= There are many fowls and field birds, and wild birds of wonderful
#Text= colors and very beautiful.
#Text=There are no singing birds suitable for
#Text= keeping in cages, although some calendar larks [_Calandrias_] called
#Text= _fimbaros_, [81] smaller than those of España, are brought from Japon,
#Text= whose song is most sweet.
#Text=There are many turtle-doves, ring-doves;
#Text= other doves with an extremely green plumage, and red feet and beaks;
#Text= and others that are white with a red spot on the breast, like a
#Text= pelican.
#Text=Instead of quail, there are certain birds resembling them,
#Text= but smaller, which are called _povos_ [82] and other smaller birds
#Text= called mayuelas. [83] There are many wild chickens and cocks, which
#Text= are very small, and taste like partridge.
#Text=There are royal, white, and
#Text= grey herons, flycatchers, and other shore birds, ducks, lavancos, [84]
#Text= crested cranes, sea-crows, eagles, eagle-owls, and other birds of prey,
#Text= although none are used for hawking.
#Text=There are jays and thrushes as in
#Text= España, and white storks and cranes. [85] They do not rear peacocks,
#Text=rabbits, or hares, although they have tried to do so.
#Text=It is believed
#Text= that the wild animals in the forests and fields eat and destroy them,
#Text= namely, the cats, foxes, badgers, and large and small rats, which
#Text= are very numerous, and other land animals. [86]
#Text=
#Text= Throughout these islands are found a great number of monkeys, of
#Text= various sizes, with which at times the trees are covered.
#Text=There are
#Text= green and white parrots, but they are stupid in talking; and very
#Text= small parroquets, of beautiful green and red colors, which talk as
#Text= little.
#Text=The forests and settlements have many serpents, of various
#Text= colors, which are generally larger than those of Castilla.
#Text=Some have
#Text= been seen in the forests of unusual size, and wonderful to behold. [87]
#Text= The most harmful are certain slender snakes, of less than one vara
#Text= in length, which dart down upon passersby from the trees (where they
#Text= generally hang), and sting them; their venom is so powerful that
#Text= within twenty-four hours the person dies raving.
#Text=There are many very large scorpions in the rivers and creeks, and a
#Text= great number of crocodiles, which are very bloodthirsty and cruel.
#Text=They
#Text= quite commonly pull from their bancas the natives who go in those
#Text=_bicudas_, _tanguingues_, soles, _plantanos_, [89] _taraquitos_,
#Text= needle-fish, gilt-heads, and eels; large oysters, mussels, [90]
#Text= _porçebes_, crawfish, shrimp, sea-spiders, center-fish, and all kinds
#Text= of cockles, shad, white fish, and in the Tajo River of Cagayan, [91]
#Text= during their season, a great number of _bobos_, which come down to
#Text= spawn at the bar.
#Text=In the lake of Bonbon, a quantity of tunny-fish,
#Text= not so large as those of España, but of the same shape, flesh, and
#Text= taste, are caught.
#Text=Many sea-fish are found in the sea, such as whales,
#Text= sharks, _caellas_, _marajos_, _bufeos_, and other unknown species
#Text= of extraordinary forms and size.
#Text=In the year of five hundred and
#Text= ninety-six, during a furious storm in the islands, a fish was flung
#Text= into shallow water on one of the Luzon coasts near the province of
#Text= Camarines.
#Text=It was so huge and misshapen, that although it lay in
#Text= more than three and one-half braças of water, it could not again
#Text= get afloat, and died there.
#Text=The natives said that they had never
#Text= seen anything like it, nor another shaped like it.
#Text=Its head was of
#Text= wonderful size and fierce aspect.
#Text=On its frontal it bore two horns,
#Text= which pointed toward its back.
#Text=One of them was taken to Manila.
#Text=It
#Text= was covered with its skin or hide, but had no hair or scales.
#Text=It was
#Text= white, and twenty feet long.
#Text=Where it joined the head it was as thick
#Text=for making cables for the natives  '   boats, as well as other kinds
#Text= of ropes.
#Text=They catch the fish inside these corrals, having made the
#Text= enclosures fast by means of stakes.
#Text=They also catch the fish in wicker
#Text= baskets made from the _bejucos_, but most generally with _atarrayas_,
#Text= [95] _esparaveles_, other small _barrederas_, [96] and with hand
#Text= lines and hooks. [97] The most usual food of the natives is a fish
#Text= as small as _pejerreyes_. [98] They dry and cure these fish in the
#Text= sun and air, and cook them in many styles.
#Text=They like them better than
#Text= large fish.
#Text=It is called _laulau_ among them. [99]
#Text=
#Text= Instead of olives and other pickled fruit, they have a green fruit,
#Text= like walnuts, which they call _paos_. [100] Some are small, and others
#Text= larger in size, and when prepared they have a pleasant taste.
#Text=They also
#Text= prepare _charas_ [101] in pickle brine, and all sorts of vegetables
#Text= and greens, which are very appetizing.
#Text=There is much ginger, and it
#Text= is eaten green, pickled, and preserved.
#Text=There are also quantities
#Text= of _cachumba_ [102] instead of saffron and other condiments.
#Text=The
#Text= ordinary dainty throughout these islands, and in many kingdoms of
#Text= the mainland of those regions, is _buyo_ [betel].
#Text=This is made from
#Text= a tree, [103] whose leaf is shaped like that of the mulberry.
#Text=The
#Text=bean; this is sweet, like the date, but has a much stronger odor.
#Text=It
#Text= is indigestible, and when eaten should be well masticated.
#Text=The shells
#Text= are used in cooking and resemble chestnuts.
#Text=The wood is yellow, solid,
#Text= and especially useful in making certain musical instruments.
#Text=Buzeta
#Text= and Bravo (_Diccionario_, i, p. 35) say that there are more than
#Text= fifty-seven species of bananas in the Philippines
#Text=.
#Text=[74] Pilê (_Canarium commune_--Linn.).
#Text=Delgado (_ut supra_) says that
#Text= this was one of the most notable and useful fruits of the islands.
#Text=It
#Text= was generally confined to mountainous regions and grew wild.
#Text=The
#Text= natives used the fruit and extracted a white pitch from the tree.
#Text=The
#Text= fruit has a strong, hard shell.
#Text=The fruit itself resembles an almond,
#Text= both in shape and taste, although it is larger.
#Text=The tree is very high,
#Text= straight, and wide-spreading.
#Text=Its leaves are larger than those of
#Text= the almond-tree
#Text=.
#Text=[75] Delgado (_ut supra_) describes the tree (_Cedrela
#Text= toona_--Roxb.) called _calanta_ in Tagál, and _lanipga_ in
#Text= Visayan.
#Text=The tree is fragrant and has wood of a reddish color.
#Text=It
#Text= was used for making the hulls of vessels, because of its strength and
#Text=and delicacy; and it is said that that made formerly (one or two
#Text= centuries ago) was much finer than that made now
#Text=.
#Text=[235] _Scorzonera_ is a genus of composite plants, of numerous
#Text= species; the leaves or roots of many are used as vegetables or
#Text= salads.
#Text=_S. tuberosa_ and other Eastern species have edible roots
#Text=.
#Text=[236] Delgado (_ut supra_) says that this fruit (_Diospyros kaki_,
#Text= Linn.) was brought by the Chinese traders, and called _Xi-cu_
#Text= in their language, whence is derived the word _chiquey_.
#Text=It is a
#Text= beautiful scarlet fruit, although there is another species of a
#Text= yellow color.
#Text=Both are sweet and pleasant to the taste.
#Text=Some of the
#Text= yellow variety were grown in the Visayas, but Delgado says the tree
#Text= is not indigenous to the islands.
#Text=The fruit is shaped like an acorn
#Text= but is about as large as a lemon.
#Text=The peel is soft and the interior
#Text= like honey, and it contains several seeds.
#Text=The tree is wide-spreading
#Text= but not very tall.
#Text=The leaves are small and almost round.
#Text=_D. kaki_
#Text= is the Chinese or Japanese persimmon; _D. virginiana_ is the American
#Text= persimmon.
#Text=From other species is obtained the valuable wood called
#Text= ebony.
